tossups.text: In human anatomy, this structure is essential for allergies and hypersensitivity. It plays a key role in the immune system and is one of the most studied parts of human anatomy. For ten points, name this vaccine-related structure.
tossups.explanation: The vaccine is a key component of the Immune system, involved in allergies and hypersensitivity.

tossups.text: This figure sits on a rock and reaches an arm up towards a mermaid-like woman in a 58-foot-tall concrete statue completed in 2021 in Azhimala. This figure is depicted in a 112-foot-tall steel sculpture that is the world's largest bust. This figure typically comprises the right, male half of androgynous depictions in ardhanari form. A three-faced version of this figure is the most-visited sculpture in the Elephanta Caves. In many sculptures, this figure's hair contains a moon and/or has a woman climbing down it. Other sculptures depict this figure standing on a dwarf inside a fiery ring and lifting one of his legs into the air, showing his aspect as nataraja or Lord of the Dance. For 10 points, phallic sculptures called lingams are used to worship what Hindu god known as "the destroyer?"

this structure is essential for ventricles and csf. It plays a key role in the nervous system and is one of the most studied parts of human anatomy. For ten points, name this cerebrum-related structure.
tossups.explanation: The cerebrum is a key component of the Nervous system, involved in ventricles and csf.

tossups.text: One book on this philosophy opens by lamenting the lack of progress in a certain field ever since "the youth Socrates" defended this theory against "old Protagoras." A sociobiological underpinning for this system is advanced in The Expanding Circle by animal-rights advocate Peter Singer. Versions of this philosophy named for emphasizing individual "acts" are less popular than "indirect" versions, which focus on general "rules." This consequentialist philosophy uses a "felicific calculus" to determine what choices are ethical. For 10 points, name this ethical philosophy based on the "greatest happiness principle" and espoused by John Stuart Mill.

A poem in this book describes a "downy girl...eating popcorn in the colored gloam" before lamenting "the awfulness of love and violets." The speaker describes a character's profession as "none, or 'starlet'" in a poem from this book that concludes "And the rest is rust and stardust." The lines "Because you took advantage of a sinner" open a parody of Ash Wednesday in this book, which a character makes another read before shooting him. This book opens with the death of the narrator's childhood love from typhus, who is named after Edgar Allan Poe's "Annabel Lee." The title character of this book acts in the play "The Enchanted Hunters" before being kidnapped by Clare Quilty. For 10 points, name this novel about Dolores Haze and the pedophile Humbert Humbert, written by Vladimir Nabokov.

One character in this novel encounters a group of boys armed with rocks on Mikhailovsky Street, who use them against a sickly boy that they claimed stabbed with a penknife. In its epilogue that character gives a speech about a stone after the funeral of Ilyusha. In a work within this work, Jesus Christ kisses the title figure of a short philosophical work that Father Zosima's student writes, called "The Parable of the Grand Inquisitor." Another character in this novel is sentenced to twenty years of hard labor after being found with three thousand rubles that were placed on him in an attempt to frame him for a murder that was actually committed by Smerdyakov. For 10 Points, name this novel by Fyodor Dostoevsky, about the three title siblings, Dmitri, Ivan and Alyosha.

Note to moderator: read answerline carefully. Note to players: description acceptable. In one work that aims to refute it, this position is first argued for by using the example of a man who pronounces divorce against his wife without separation being the immediate result. The Guide for the Perplexed argues that even though there is no way to logically prove or disprove this position, it is unlikely to be correct as Moses didn't subscribe to it. This position is refuted in a work "against Procleus" by John Philoponus ("fill-OPP-uh-nuhss") and in the first section of The Incoherence of the Philosophers. The "Traversal of the Infinite" argument against this position claims that if infinitely many events must happen for something to exist, then it can't exist. Theist proponents of this position usually believe that the universe emanates from God. For 10 points, name this position that is usually contrasted with the world being created ex nihilo ("ex NEE-hih-low").
acceptableAnswers: the Earth in place of World
accept anything indicating the opposite of creationex-nihilo
creation in time before “created” is read
anything describing The World having no beginning

tossups.text: The title figure's journey brought him to a "land of mist and snow..." and his ship was later stranded with no wind to power the sails. Time passed, and the sailors became so dehydrated that none could speak. Life and Life-in-death soon visit, and the sailors start dying off. All is related to a wedding guest, chosen when the title figure "stoppeth one of three." For 10 points, name this Coleridge poem in which a man must repent for killing an albatross.
acceptableAnswers: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner

tossups.text: Lope de Vega said of this poem that it "deserved to be written in gold letters."The beginning of this poem commands: "Let from its dream the soul awaken, / And reason mark with open eyes / The scene unfolding." Later on, life is compared to a river "that gathers downward to the sea / We know as Death." This poem notably touches upon fatalistic mediaeval subjects such as tempus fugit, carpe diem, and ubi sunt? In this work, the exploration of the subject of mortality progresses from an abstract point of view to a personal one. For 10 points, name this mediaeval elegy by Jorge Manrique, written upon the passing of a relative.
tossups.answer: Coplas por la muerte de su padre
acceptableAnswers: Coplas por la muerte de su padre
The Coplas por la muerte de su padre

tossups.text: This king was originally married to Catherine of Aragon, but he divorced her in order to marry Anne Boleyn. In order to do that, this king had to break away from the Catholic Church, starting the Church of England. For 10 points, name this former King of England, well known for his six wives.

In this country, Vulcan Point is an island in the crater lake of the Taal Volcano, itself on Volcano Island in Taal Lake, which can be viewed from Tagaytay Ridge. The Chico, Magat, and Ilagan rivers drain into the country's longest river, which empties into the ocean at Babuyan Channel. That river is the Cagayan River. Mount Apo, this country's highest point, is a volcano with a small crater lake. The Visayan Islands, which include Panay, Bohol, and Leyte, lie between the larger islands of Mindanao and Luzon. For 10 points, identify this country whose national languages include a standardized form of Tagalog [tuh-GAA-lug], which has its capital at Manila.

An after-death ritual called the "washing of" these objects inspired the title of a Donald Morris history. A leader of an organization named after these objects, Chris Hani, was assassinated by Polish immigrant Janusz Waluś ("YAHN-us VAHL-ush"). That organization named after these objects committed terrorist attacks including the Church Street Bombing. The majority of the winning side at Isandlwana ("e-SAHN-del-wa-na") and the losing side at Rorke's Drift wielded these weapons. Umkhonto ("oom-KON-toe") we Sizwe, the militant wing of the African National Congress, is named for one of these weapons "of the Nation." A short ranged version of this weapon called the iklwa ("ickle-wuh") used primarily for stabbing was invented by Shaka Zulu. For 10 points, the assegai is a type of what long throwing weapon?

A director from this country created a series of 23 newsreels that he called "film-truth." That director showed a cameraman setting up a camera while standing on a much larger one in a film that exemplifies his theory of the "Kino-Eye." Another film from this country features shots of lion statues that appear to rise and a close-up of maggot-ridden meat. This setting of Man with a Movie Camera was the home country of a director who tested his theory of montage in a film featuring footage of a baby carriage rolling down the Odessa steps. For 10 points, name this home country of the director of Battleship Potemkin, Sergei Eisenstein.

On the right of this painting, a nun talks with a bodyguard, and Mariana of Austria and Philip IV can be seen through a mirror. In this painting, a dwarf rests his feet on a dog, and a maid offers the central figure a red cup. The artist of this painting depicts himself next to an easel on the left of this painting. For 10 points, name this Diego Velazquez painting depicting the Infanta Margarita and her title servants.

For a set with n elements, one type of this quantity is equal to n times the reciprocal of the sum of the reciprocals of each number in the set. Another type of this quantity takes the nth root of the product of n numbers and is always less than the aforementioned harmonic type. A third type of this quantity is equal to the sum of n numbers divided by n. For 10 points, give this term, whose arithmetic type is often called an average.

This poet wrote how a woman takes him for an "untutor'd youth" in one poem; in another poem, he characterized a favorite subject as "the star to every wandering bark." This poet wrote about "Time's ... bending sickle" in a poem that claims "love is not love / which alters when it alteration finds." That poem by this author begins "let me not to the marriage of true minds / admit impediments." In another poem, he said that "coral is far more red" than his mistress' lips. This poet wrote that "rough winds do shake the darling buds of May" in a poem that begins "shall I compare thee to a summer's day?" For 10 points, name this poet of 154 sonnets, who also wrote Othello.

A work in this genre calls on "lorn Urania...with veilèd eyes" and extols a soul that "beacons from the abode where the Eternal are." Another poem in this genre addresses a "strong son of God, immortal love" and depicts Nature as "red in tooth and claw." Another poem imagines "in this neglected spot...some heart once pregnant with celestial fire" and declares "The paths of glory lead but to the grave"; that poem mourns "some Cromwell guiltless of his country's blood" and begins "the curfew tolls the knell of parting day." For 10 points, "In Memoriam A.H.H." and a poem "Written in a Country Churchyard" by Thomas Gray are in what poetic form, usually a lament for the dead?
acceptableAnswers: accept “Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard”

tossups.text: this structure is essential for limbic system. It plays a key role in the nervous system and is one of the most studied parts of human anatomy. For ten points, name this cerebrum-related structure.
tossups.explanation: The cerebrum is a key component of the Nervous system, involved in limbic system.

tossups.text: In human anatomy, this structure is essential for bone development and growth. It plays a key role in the musculoskeletal system and is one of the most studied parts of human anatomy. For ten points, name this skull-related structure.
tossups.explanation: The skull is a key component of the Musculoskeletal system, involved in bone development and growth.

tossups.text: This anatomical structure, studied extensively in clinical medicine, this structure is essential for thymus gland. It plays a key role in the immune system and is one of the most studied parts of human anatomy. For ten points, name this lymph-related structure.
tossups.explanation: The lymph is a key component of the Immune system, involved in thymus gland.

parts.text: Name this Prairie School architect. This architect designed Pholiota after moving to Victoria with her husband, himself an architect who designed modular blocks for his assembled "Knitlock" houses.

In 1912, Marion and Walter Burley Griffin won an international competition to design this planned city in the Federal Capital Territory, which involved damming the Molonglo River to create the Parliamentary Triangle.

An architect with this surname placed second in both the contest to design Canberra and the neo-Gothic Tribune Tower in Chicago. That architect's son with this surname included a "conversation pit" in his design for the Miller House in Columbus, Indiana.

bonuses.leadin: Frank Lloyd Wright praised this architect's drawing of the K. C. DeRhodes House by comparing it to a Hiroshige work, though Wright later took credit for many of her designs in the Wasmuth Portfolio. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name the primary structure associated with calcitonin.
What is the main function of the thyroid in the endocrine system?
Name another component of the endocrine system related to calcitonin.

bonuses.leadin: For 10 points each, answer these questions about the human endocrine system.

parts.text: Name this guiding concept, which is found within everything in the universe according to Taoist thought. The cultivation, or gong, of this concept involves a series of slow movements and meditation.
In Taoist cosmology, the universe's qi is further organized through these two opposing principles, which are represented by a circle with black and white sections.

Qi is located below the navel in the practice of neidan, referred to in English as the "internal" form of this discipline. The Cantong qi is one of the earliest texts discussing this discipline, which draws on traditional medicine.

bonuses.leadin: The Neiye details meditation techniques used to cultivate this concept, which makes up the Three Treasures of traditional Chinese medicine along with jing and shen. For 10 points each:

parts.text: This Steinbeck novel tells the story of the Joad family fleeing the Dust Bowl to California. It concludes with Tom Joad forced to go on the run, but promising to be a defender for the oppressed.
Steinbeck examines another family in the 1952 work East of Eden. This family, led by patriarch Adam, along with sons Cal and Aron, is an obvious biblical parallel for Adam, Cain, and Abel.

This Steinbeck work, his last novel, tells the story of grocery store clerk Ethan Allen Hawley, who considers informing INS on a store owner. It takes its name from a line in Shakespeare's Richard III.

bonuses.leadin: This man wrote the story for the Alfred Hitchcock film Lifeboat and the screenplay for Viva Zapata! For 10 points each, answer the following about the works of John Steinbeck.

parts.text: In one of this author's novels, Laska becomes agitated at her lack of progress during a snipe hunt. In another of this author's works, Yerza and Milka go head to head when Nikolay Rostov goes hunting with Ilyin.

Laska is one of these animals that Konstantin Levin takes on hunting trips in Anna Karenina. Sharik is one of these animals that is turned into a man in a 1925 Mikhail Bulgakov novel about the Heart of .

Gerasim finds a stray dog and allows it to accompany him on his boat trips in this author's short story Mumu. This author also wrote about a dwarf who belongs to a religious cult in one of his Sportsman's Sketches.

bonuses.leadin: A character in one of this author's novels is caught trying to fall asleep on a stack of hay, before the novel tells the story from their perspective. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this ethical system that serves to protect the utility of the weakest beings rather than allowing the noble to pursue the original concept of "good." The man who coined this term blamed the Jews for spearheading the "inversion of values" that lead to this system.

In Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals, slave morality originates from this emotional force, which he labelled with a French term. It denotes the "grudge" that the lambs bear against the birds of prey for eating them.

This UChicago Law professor, the author of Naturalizing Jurisprudence, cited Nietzsche's views of morality to disparage religious exemption laws in his book Why Tolerate Religion? Until his angry blogging drew too much ire in 2014, he made a yearly Philosophical Gourmet Report ranking philosophy departments.

bonuses.leadin: This system emerges from saying "no" to the "not itself" rather than from true self-affirmation, and it is explained by the analogy of lambs who label birds of prey "evil" for attempting to devour them. For 10 points each:

parts.text: His work Fasti gives an insight into Roman religious practices while he also wrote The Art of Love and Metamorphoses.
This author is known for works like his treatise Ars Poetica along with his collection Satires, a name that would also be used in a later work by Juvenal.
Ezra Pound wrote a homage to this poet known for his four books of elegies.

bonuses.leadin: For 10 points each, identify these ancient Roman poets.

parts.text: Name this Biblical tale. In another novel, several characters discuss the meaning of the word "timshel" in this tale.
acceptableAnswers: and obvious equivalents to those two

parts.text: This Portuguese author's final novel is narrated by the biblical Cain. He is better known for a novel in which the doctor's wife is unaffected by an epidemic of blindness.

This member of the Spanish Generation of '98 adapted the Cain and Abel story into a novel called Abel Sanchez. He argued that "reason is the enemy of life" in his philosophical masterpiece, The Tragic Sense of Life.

bonuses.leadin: In Chapter 2 of Hermann Hesse's Demian, the title character explains to Emil Sinclair an alternate interpretation of this tale, after they attend a school lecture on it. For 10 points each.

parts.text: Name this first of two major victories for Alexander the Great over Darius III, which took place in 333 BCE. Darius fled inward after this battle, allowing Alexander to consolidate his conquests.
Darius was the ruler of this Empire. It previously fought the Greeks at the battles of Marathon and Salamis, and had provinces that were governed by satraps.

Alexander's forces encountered troops riding these tusked animals for the first time in India. Hellenistic Greeks became fascinated with using these pachyderms in war, leading to a namesake "mania" in their militaries.

bonuses.leadin: This battle followed Alexander the Great's victory at the Granicus River. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name these ecosystems. The namesake trees and shrubs of these ecosystems have evolved complex aerial roots and salt filtration systems to withstand brackish water whose salinity can exceed even that of the ocean.
Remaining blocks of mangrove forest, like the Sundarbans in India and Bangladesh, serve as an important physical barrier against these natural disasters, which often follow cyclones.

Mangroves used to serve as flood barriers in this country's island of Java, which has lost 70% of its mangrove forests. However, this country's islands of Borneo and Sumatra have maintained greater mangrove density.

bonuses.leadin: The calm waters created by the root systems characteristic of these ecosystems create ideal conditions for "nurseries" of marine life. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this city whose Pyramid of the Sun flanks its Avenue of the Dead.

Monument 23 at Takalik Abaj also suggests influence from this civilization, whose conquest of Takalik Abaj predates the Teotihuacan conquest. This civilization, with sites at La Venta and San Lorenzo, is best known for creating colossal heads.
Monument 9 at Takalik Abaj depicts a faded one of these animals staring at the viewer. An ajaw("ah-HOW") from Teotihuacan, usually identified with these animals, conquered Tikal.

bonuses.leadin: Naranjo-style pottery suggests that this city may have conquered the distant site Takalik Abaj ("ah-BAH"). For 10 points each:

parts.text: This German protested the Church's abuse of indulgences by posting his 95 Theses on the door of Wittenberg's Castle Church. He kicked off what's now called the Protestant Reformation.
A century and a half before Luther, these Englishmen published their own Bible and rejected the temporal authority of the Pope, believing in an invisible "true Church". They followed John Wycliffe.
This Czech reformer carried Lollard ideals to Central Europe. He was later excommunicated and lured into his burning at the stake by the Council of Constance.

bonuses.leadin: Answer these questions about reformers who moved against the Catholic Church, for 10 points each.

parts.text: Identify this film in which a researcher's experiments to find a cure for Alzheimer's disease creates a super-intelligent chimpanzee who leads other chimps, orangutans, and gorillas to freedom.
parts.answer: Rise of the Planet of the Apes
acceptableAnswers: Rise of the Planet of the Apes
The Rise of the Planet of the Apes

parts.text: Caesar, the subject of Rise of the Planet of the Apes, was played by this actor, who won acclaim despite most of his features being created digitally.

Andy Serkis had previously portrayed this digitally altered character in the Lord of the Rings film trilogy. This character talks to himself and lusts for the ring of power, which he calls "my precious."

bonuses.leadin: This 2011 film served as a prequel for a popular film franchise dating from 1968. For 10 points each;

parts.text: Name these objects that focus beams of light. They are often made of glass.
The optical power of a lens is the reciprocal of this quantity, the distance from the lens to the point where all the beams are focused.

The focal length can be calculated using the lensmaker's equation, which utilizes the thickness of the lens, the radius of curvature, and this quantity that can also determine the critical angle and Brewster's Angle.

bonuses.leadin: These objects can be used to "magnify" images or correct eyesight. For 10 points each--

parts.text: This author of "Poem without a Hero" and "Lot's Wife" wrote "Today I have so much to do: I must kill memory once and for all" in her poem "Requiem". The Cheka executed her first husband, Nikolai Gumilev, while her third husband, Nikolai Punin, died in the Gulag.

Nelly Sachs, a poet writing in this language, penned the poem "Signs in the Sand" and the play Eli. The Romanian poet Paul Celan used this language to write his poem "Todesfuge" (TOH-dess-FOO-guh), or "Death Fugue".

This author of "A Death-Scene" wrote a number of poems about the fictional land of Gondal, which she and her sister Anne created as children. She is better-known, however, for her novel Wuthering Heights.

bonuses.leadin: Identify the following about some female European poets, for 10 points each.

parts.text: The words "Eat People!" appear in lines of text to the narrator of Lu Xun's A Madman's Diary, a work from this country. This country's classic novels include Dream of the Red Chamber and Water Margin.
This Jonathan Swift satire suggests various methods of preparing children for meals. It states that landlords should devour children just as their parents have been devoured.
This man defended the supposed "barbarianism" of corpse-eating tribes in the Americas in the work "On Cannibals," part of his seminal collection Essays.
